About the Cover

PAGTUGDÓK

About the Cover

The cover presents the title of this portfolio, “Pagtugdók,” a Bicolano term that means construction. Shown on the left side is the image of a construction worker, while on the right side is a pre-service teacher. Though they work in different fields, both embody “the art of building dreams,” which serves as the tagline of this portfolio. The construction worker builds dream houses, while the teacher builds a dream future. Both crafts require patience and dedication, and their outputs are built not instantly but step-by-step. In the same way, this portfolio is a product of a long process of effort, with each artifact carefully completed not at once but gradually.

00 — Introduction

Introduction

Builder of Others' Dream

This portfolio is dedicated to my father, whose hard work as a construction worker continues to provide strength and support for our family. Growing up, I often wondered why those who build strong houses for others struggle to build the same for themselves. He constructs dream houses, yet our own dream house remains only a dream. In many ways, teachers are also construction workers. They build dreams by honing the minds and character of the young generation, yet they are undervalued within the very educational system they serve. They always aim for the development of their students, but their own personal and professional development is often ignored because of the demanding responsibilities, inequitable compensation, and other systemic issues.

Despite these realities, I still aspire to become a “construction worker” who can build intelligent and compassionate individuals. I remember when I applied for a scholarship at Ateneo de Naga University, the letter of intent I submitted contained this line: "There is no money in teaching…you will not be able to raise your family out of poverty through the teaching profession.” If this claim is true, then teaching is indeed like being a construction worker—often underpaid and sometimes undervalued.

BUILDER'S GOAL

This portfolio aims to document the author’s learning progress and outputs throughout the semester in the course Assessment of Student Learning II. It also serves as an avenue for the author to reflect on his learning experiences and to share the knowledge he has gained, its significance to him as a pre-service teacher, and the ways in which it can be applied in his future profession.

01 — Pagkalót
No.01

Excavating and Positioning the Posts

Pagkalót

Finished on 27 January 2026

Builder's Goal

To create a Table of Specifications (TOS), construct test questions aligned with it, and develop an item locator that ensures reliability, fairness, validity, and alignment of the assessment with the learning objectives.

Artifact 1: Table of Specifications, Test Questions, and Item Locator

In constructing a house, everything begins with excavation, in which the soil is assessed to determine whether it can support the weight of the structure. This process prepares the ground and ensures that the house will stand firm and stable over time. My parents told me that our humble house was built gradually. During the first two years of their marriage, while they still had no child, they stayed at their parent’s house as they worked hard to build their own. Little by little, my father would buy sacks of cement and reinforcement bars each month and would construct the posts one at a time. Their experience has something to teach us about building strong foundations. It tells us that construction should never be rushed.

Similarly, in assessment development, teachers should never rush creating test questions. In constructing this artifact, I learned the importance of having a “question bank” where teachers can regularly write one or two test items each day. In this way, teachers can avoid cramming the test questions to be used at the end of the grading period. Instead, they only need to review and select appropriate questions based on the Table of Specifications (TOS). The TOS serves as the foundation of assessment development. Therefore, it must be prepared carefully because it acts as the blueprint of the assessment. It ensures that the content of the test aligns with the intended learning objectives, corresponds to the number of instructional hours, and targets higher-order thinking skills. Just as excavation ensures the stability of a house before construction begins, creating proper TOS establishes stability and direction before constructing the actual test questions. Furthermore, every test item must be properly arranged in increasing order of complexity, making the item locator equally significant. It is like how every post in a house must be accurately measured and properly placed to ensure the strength and balance of the structure.

Through this artifact, I learned that teachers must invest time and effort in developing assessments because assessment does not merely measure the effectiveness of instruction; it is an essential part of the instructional process itself. In creating this artifact, I became more detail-oriented in ensuring that the test questions demonstrate reliability, fairness, and content, instruction, and face validity. This experience taught me that quality assessments are achieved through careful preparation rather than rushed work. As a pre-service teacher, this artifact deepened my understanding of teacher’s responsibility not only to deliver instruction effectively but also to design reliable and valid assessments that support student learning.

02 — Paglanób
No.02

Assembling the Walls

Paglanób

Finished on 24 February 2026

Builder's Goal

To write a position essay that critically examines and defends the claim “Cheating by all means is good” using philosophical and evidence-based arguments.

Artifact 2: Position Essay — "Cheating by All Means is Good"

After establishing the foundation, the next step in building a house is constructing the walls. In our house, the main structure is made of cement walls, yet they are not smoothly finished. Because of this, during rainy season, continuous rainfall causes the walls to absorb water. Despite this, they remain strong and standing. Life is not always filled with sunny days; storms and heavy rains will always come. Still, the walls are prepared to withstand these harsh conditions. In the same way, teachers should not always make everything easy for their students. Instead, they must help students become like strong walls that are capable of facing difficult questions and challenging situations. Through this, students learn how to think beyond and develop the confidence to face real-life challenges.

This is what Artifact 2 taught me: the value of critical thinking. Challenges do not weaken the mind; rather, they sharpen it, just as walls become stronger as they endure adverse conditions. In this artifact, defending an idea that is generally considered wrong pushed me to think critically. Writing a position essay about the claim, “Cheating by all means is good,” challenged not only my logical reasoning but also my personal principles and values. Fortunately, during the time I wrote this essay, we were discussing utilitarianism in our philosophy class. Because of this, I used utilitarianism as the philosophical basis for my argument. This experience showed me that thought-provoking performance tasks allow students to connect and integrate learning from different subject areas.

Through this artifact, I realized that meaningful learning happens when students are challenged to analyze and justify their ideas rather than simply memorize information. I learned that creating activities that promote critical thinking, reasoning, and interdisciplinary learning is important, as effective teaching is not about giving students all the answers but about guiding them to think independently, question critically, and express their perspectives confidently.

03 — Pagsalóg
No.03

Laying the Floor

Pagsalóg

Finished on 05 March 2026

Builder's Goal

To construct a performance-based task prompt using the GRASPS model that includes a clear description of the nature of the final product, an instruction of what the students are required to accomplish, as well as the criteria to be used to judge the final product.

Artifact 3: Performance-Based Task Prompt Using the GRASPS Model

In building a house, the floor must be properly leveled and reinforced to ensure that it remains flat and able to withstand time. In our house, it is noticeable that the floor has become uneven, especially in the middle portion where it seems to slowly sink. There are also visible cracks in some areas. My father explained that it is because our floor was built without reinforcement bars. It was simply made from a mixture of gravel stones, sand, and cement. Because of this, after more than two decades, signs of weakening and damage have naturally appeared. This situation clearly shows the importance of having a strong support system in any structure.

This idea can also be applied in performance-based assessment. Just as a floor cannot maintain its strength without proper reinforcement, students cannot successfully accomplish performance tasks without adequate guidance from teachers. Teachers must provide clear instructions, criteria, and sufficient background information so that students can fully understand what is expected of them. Without these, students may become confused, produce low-quality outputs, or fail to demonstrate their true abilities. Hence, a well-written performance-based task prompt is essential for providing both students and teachers with clear expectations. This can be achieved by defining the goal, role, audience, situation, product, and standards (GRASPS) of the performance task clearly so that all components are properly understood.

In this artifact, I learned that support systems are essential not only in physical structures but also in the learning process. Proper guidance makes the implementation of performance-based assessment successful. As a pre-service teacher, I realized that one of my responsibilities is to become a source of support for my future students by providing them with clear instructions and guidelines in every assessment and learning activity.

04 — Pag-atóp
No.04

Roofing the Structure

Pag-atóp

Finished on 14 April 2026

Builder's Goal

To create analytical and holistic rubrics that provide clear, fair, and consistent criteria for assessing students in a process-based performance task.

Artifact 4: Analytical and Holistic Rubrics

The roof serves as protection for a house. It shields the entire structure from external conditions such as heat, rain, and wind. In our home, however, roofing is a concern not during rainy season but during summer. Since we do not have a ceiling, the heat from the sun directly penetrates the roof, making the house feel like an enclosed oven during the hottest part of the day. The temperature inside becomes uncomfortable and at times even unbearable. Because of this, I preferred face-to-face classes over online learning, as our house is not conducive for virtual classes. It is ironic because my father specializes in installing different kinds of ceilings, yet we cannot afford to install one in our house. This situation highlights how the absence of adequate protective structures can significantly affect the quality of daily living. Likewise, in assessment, the absence of rubrics can significantly compromise the quality of evaluation.

In Artifact 4, we created an analytical and holistic rubric for a product-based performance task. The rubric functions much like the roof of an assessment. It provides protection by ensuring that the evaluation of performance-based assessments remains objective, fair, and consistent. Just as a roof shields a house from external conditions, a well-designed rubric safeguards the assessment from subjectivity, inconsistency, and bias. The analytical rubric breaks down student performance into specific criteria, allowing for a detailed and focused evaluation of each dimension of learning. In contrast, the holistic rubric assesses overall performance as a single, integrated judgment.

I learned, through creating this artifact, the importance of carefully selecting appropriate words for each level descriptor to clearly show the gradation within the rubric. I also realized that having many criteria is not necessary. What matters more is ensuring that the criteria comprehensively capture all essential qualities of the performance or product. In addition, I learned that descriptors must be clear and concise to ensure accurate and consistent interpretation. I have learned that well-constructed rubrics are essential tools in assessment. They provide transparency in grading, clarify expectations for students, and guide them toward achieving learning outcomes more effectively. Like a strong roof, rubrics complete the structure of assessment by offering protection against bias, direction for improvement, and fairness in evaluation.

05 — Pagkudál
No.05

Installing the Fence

PAGKUDÁL

Finished on 30 April 2026

Builder's Goal

To develop an ana-holistic rubric for a product-based performance task.

Artifact 5: Ana-Holistic Rubric

A fence defines boundaries and offers protection. Our house is surrounded by a bamboo fence constructed by my father. He arranged each bamboo pole with equal spacing and uniform height and fixed them together one by one. Its purpose was not really to protect us from thieves but to prevent stray dogs and chickens from entering our yard and damaging our plants. Individually, each bamboo pole may seem insignificant, yet when combined, they form a strong barrier of protection.

This can be related to an ana-holistic rubric, which integrates the strengths of both analytical and holistic rubrics. The analytical component resembles the individual bamboo poles because it breaks down a performance task into specific criteria. Meanwhile, the holistic component mirrors the fence as a whole, capturing the overall quality and impact of students’ performance. Just as the bamboo fence safeguards our home, an ana-holistic rubric safeguards the assessment from subjective and inconsistent scoring. However, unlike the fence that defines boundaries, ana-holistic rubric gives not a limit on students' performance or product, but rather a clear standard on what is expected from them. In developing Artifact 5, an ana-holistic rubric for a product-based performance task, I realized the importance of precision and clarity in rubric construction. The descriptors must be specific, comprehensive, and easily understandable so that students are properly guided in creating their outputs. Likewise, the language used in the rubric should be carefully chosen to avoid confusion and misinterpretation.

As a student, I used to ignore rubrics because I felt that some teachers were not always faithful in using them when they score our performance tasks. However, through this artifact, I realized the true value of rubrics. Rubrics provide students with a clear understanding of how their work will be evaluated, helping them become more aware of the expectations and standards they need to meet. At the same time, rubrics facilitate the scoring process for teachers and ensure objectivity, fairness, and consistency. They serve a complete package for scoring that benefits both students and teachers.

06 — Pagpíntura
No.06

Finishing with Paint

Pagpíntura

Finished on 05 May 2026

Builder's Goal

To design and administer a sociometric questionnaire to a specific class section and to construct positive and negative sociometric matrices based on its results to analyze social relationships within the class.

Artifact 6: Sociometry

Paint adds beauty to a house. It enhances its appearance. Our house has no paint. It remains plain and unfinished. Yet, it is often said that the true beauty of a home does not come from its architecture or color but from the relationships among the people living in it. Similarly, in a classroom, it is not the physical appearance that gives color and life to the environment, but rather the interactions and relationships among the students that truly define the class atmosphere.

In this artifact, I wanted to focus on the affective domain. Thus, I decided to create a sociometry. Since I had no knowledge about how to conduct and present a sociometric study, I conducted research to better understand the process. I discovered that sociometry can be carried out through a sociometric questionnaire administered to a specific class, where students identify classmates who best fit the descriptions in each question. I also learned that the gathered data may be presented through sociometric matrices or diagrams. I chose to use matrices because they are less complicated and easier to interpret than diagrams. To gather data, I asked my younger sister, who is a Grade 11 student, if I could use her class as participants for the study. Fortunately, she immediately agreed and shared the questionnaire through their group chat. Even though they were already on vacation, several of her classmates still responded to the questionnaire, including almost half of the class.

While creating the sociometric matrices, I began to notice patterns in the students’ relationships. Some students appeared to be more socially connected and frequently chosen by their classmates, while others received fewer selections. Through this process, I realized how important sociometry can be for teachers. It may help them understand the social dynamics within the classroom and identify students who may feel isolated. This information can guide teachers in creating activities, seating arrangements, and interventions to promote inclusivity and positive relationships among students. From this experience, I learned that teaching is not only about delivering academic content but also about understanding students’ emotions and relationships within the classroom.

07 — Pagsuyab
No.07

Expanding the Structure

Pagsuyab

Finished on 09 May 2026

Builder's Goal

To conduct a mini-qualitative study investigating the status of portfolio assessment in public schools in Camarines Sur using a short-response questionnaire as a data-gathering tool.

Artifact 7: Mini-Study on Portfolio Assessment

Our house has many extensions that were gradually built whenever resources became available. These additions mean a continuous development. Similarly, in the learning process, we can also extend our learnings. This development can happen when we move beyond mere acquiring knowledge and begin applying what we have learned into action. Learning must not end with questioning and understanding. This realization became the inspiration behind conducting this mini-study.

I felt that merely knowing what a portfolio is was not enough. I wanted to understand how portfolio assessment is actually practiced by teachers. Despite the limited time available, I decided to conduct this study because I wanted to explore the awareness and status of portfolio assessment within the locality where I will most likely serve as a future teacher. Through this study, I discovered that many teachers are indeed using portfolios as part of their assessment practices. However, they only utilize an “informal” kind of portfolio. Two of my respondents were my former teachers. Through their responses, I realized that the portfolio I had known since elementary was not actually a portfolio but rather a compilation of our outputs and activities.

Although this study was small in scope and my recommendations would not reach the Department of Education, it encouraged me to begin with actions within my capacity by promoting proper understanding of portfolio assessment to my participants and other teachers I know. I realized that portfolio assessment can serve as a complement to written tests and performance tasks, as it allows teachers to assess not only student outputs but also their learning process, creativity, and development.

Bio

Den Errol A. Tejero is a second-year BSE Science student at Ateneo de Naga University. He comes from a humble family in the municipality of Camaligan. He is the eldest and only son among three siblings, raised by his father, who works as a construction worker, and his mother, who manages a small variety store.

His educational journey began at Tarosanan-San Francisco Elementary School, where his dream of becoming an educator first took shape. He later completed his junior high school education at Camaligan National High School and pursued senior high school at Naga City Science High School. Believing that education is the clearest path toward a more stable life, he continues to persevere in his studies and aspirations. Today, he strives to become a different kind of builder, a construction worker not of physical structures but of a better future.

Beyond academics, he actively serves in their parish community at St. Anthony of Padua Parish as a member of the Youth Ministry and a former member of the Ministry of Lectors. He also currently serves as the second-year level representative of the Samahang Tagapagtaguyod ng Edukasyong Pilipino (STEP).

A dreamer, a builder, and a future teacher.

WHAT'S NEXT?Integration
Good teaching is more a giving of right questions than a giving of right answers. ~ Josef Albers Assessment is much like building a house. It requires a strong foundation, careful planning, protection of its structure, and continuous improvement. Through the various artifacts I have created, I have come to understand the essential role of assessment in both teaching and learning. Assessment does not merely measure performance; it supports learning and instruction. For learners, assessment provides feedback on their strengths and areas for improvement. For teachers, it serves as a guide to evaluate the effectiveness of instruction, identify learning gaps, and even understand classroom dynamics. This portfolio has helped me realize that assessment is not a separate task in teaching. Rather, it is interconnected with planning, instruction, and student development. As a future teacher, I aim to design assessments that are reliable, fair, valid, and inclusive. My goal is to create a classroom environment where assessment is used not only for grading but also as a tool that enhances learning, supports student growth, and fosters continuous improvement for both learners and instruction.
